def: Four guarantees that make database writes trustworthy: **A**tomicity (all-or-nothing), **C**onsistency (valid states only), **I**solation (concurrent writes don't corrupt each other), **D**urability (survives crashes).
An LLM that can use **tools** and take multi-step actions — call APIs, query databases, run code — looping until a task is done.
The most popular **orchestration** tool. Schedules and sequences data pipelines as DAGs (graphs of tasks), with retries and monitoring.
Application Programming Interface — a defined way for programs to talk to each other. You 'call an API' to request data or a service over the internet.
A compact, binary, **row-based** file format with built-in schema. Popular in streaming/Kafka and where schemas evolve frequently.
The three big **cloud** providers (Amazon, Microsoft, Google). They rent computing power, storage, and ready-made data/AI services over the internet.
Re-running a pipeline for past dates it missed or needs reprocessed (e.g. after fixing a bug in the logic).
The relaxed alternative to ACID used by many NoSQL systems: **B**asically **A**vailable, **S**oft state, **E**ventually consistent. Trades instant consistency for availability/scale.
Processing data in chunks on a schedule (e.g. every night), as opposed to continuously. Simpler and cheaper than streaming.
Google Cloud's serverless data **warehouse**. No clusters to manage; billed mainly by the amount of data each query scans.
Data too large or fast for a single machine to handle, requiring distributed tools like Spark. Often described by 'the 3 Vs': Volume, Velocity, Variety.
A Spark optimisation: when one table is small, copy it to every worker to avoid an expensive shuffle during a join.
In a distributed system, during a network partition you can't have both perfect **Consistency** and **Availability** — you must choose one. See [[ACID]].
Capturing inserts/updates/deletes from a source database in near-real-time by reading its change log — an efficient way to do incremental loads.
Renting computers, storage, and software over the internet instead of buying your own. Where nearly all modern data and AI work happens.
A group of computers working together as one system (e.g. a Spark cluster) to process data in parallel.
Storing each column's values together (vs whole rows). Makes analytical queries fast and compress well. See [[Parquet]].
The maximum amount of text (in **tokens**) an LLM can consider at once — its short-term working memory.
The four basic data operations: **C**reate, **R**ead, **U**pdate, **D**elete.
Common Table Expression — a named temporary result in SQL (`WITH name AS (...)`) that makes complex queries readable and reusable.
Directed Acyclic Graph — tasks connected by dependencies with a direction and no loops. How Airflow models a workflow.
When incoming data's statistics slowly change over time, silently degrading models or reports. Detected by monitoring distributions.
The person who builds and maintains the systems (pipelines, warehouses) that move and shape data so others can use it reliably.
Cheap, vast storage (usually object storage like S3) holding raw data of any type. Flexible, but can become a disorganised 'data swamp'.
A blend of lake + warehouse: cheap file storage with a table layer (Delta/Iceberg) adding reliability (ACID), so it's cheap *and* trustworthy.
A focused subset of a warehouse serving one team or subject area (e.g. a finance mart).
An automated flow that moves data from sources to destinations, transforming it along the way. See [[ETL]].
A database optimised for analytics: structured tables, fast SQL over huge data. Examples: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift.
A programmable table of data with rows and columns. The core object in pandas (one machine) and Spark (many machines).
A popular tool for doing the 'T' in ELT: transforming data inside a warehouse using SQL, with tests, docs, and version control.
Machine learning using neural networks with many layers. Excels at images, audio, and language. Powers modern AI. See [[Neural network]].
A storage layer that adds database reliability (ACID transactions, time travel, MERGE) to files in a data lake. Core to the lakehouse.
Deliberately duplicating/pre-joining data to make reads faster by avoiding joins. Common in analytical warehouses (star schema).
A table of descriptive context you slice data by (product, date, customer). Joins to a fact table in a star schema.
A list of numbers (a vector) representing the *meaning* of text/image. Similar meanings have nearby vectors. Powers semantic search and RAG.
**E**xtract, **T**ransform, **L**oad — the pattern for moving and reshaping data. ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw then transforms (modern cloud default).
A processing guarantee that each event is handled once — no loss, no duplicates. The hardest and most desirable delivery semantic in streaming.
The central table in a star schema holding measurable events/metrics (amounts, counts) plus keys to dimensions. See [[Dimension table]].
A system that computes, stores, and serves the same ML 'features' consistently for both model training and live prediction.
Further-training an existing model on your own data to teach it new behaviour/style. See [[LoRA]]. Contrast with [[RAG]].
AI that *creates* new content — text, images, audio, code — rather than only classifying or predicting. See [[LLM]].
Global Interpreter Lock — a Python limitation letting only one thread run Python code at a time. Work around with multiprocessing or C-backed libraries.
The standard tool for version-controlling code — tracking changes, collaborating, and saving history. GitHub hosts Git repositories online.
What a single row in a fact table represents (e.g. 'one row per order line'). The most important data-modelling decision.
Graphics Processing Unit — hardware that does massively parallel maths, essential for training and running deep-learning models.
When an LLM confidently states something false. The central reliability problem of LLMs; reduced with RAG, citations, and guardrails.
High-Level Design — the bird's-eye system view: major components, data flow, and big technology choices. See [[LLD]].
A pipeline is idempotent if running it many times gives the same result as once — so retries never duplicate data. Achieved with upserts/partition overwrites.
Identity & Access Management — controls who can do what to which cloud resource. Follow 'least privilege': grant only the minimum needed.
Processing only new/changed data since the last run (using a watermark), instead of reprocessing everything (full load).
A sorted structure that lets a database find rows fast without scanning the whole table — like a book's index. Speeds reads, slows writes.
JavaScript Object Notation — a human-readable, flexible text format for data, common in APIs. Basically nested key-value pairs and lists.
A distributed, durable, replayable log for **streaming** events. Decouples producers from consumers via topics and partitions. See [[Streaming]].
Low-Level Design — the detailed design of a component: schemas, classes, APIs, algorithms. The zoomed-in counterpart to [[HLD]].
Large Language Model — a generative AI trained on huge text to understand and produce language. Examples: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama.
Efficient fine-tuning: train tiny add-on matrices instead of all weights (cheap, swappable). QLoRA adds quantization to fit on one GPU.
Computers learning patterns from examples instead of being explicitly programmed with rules. A subset of AI; superset of deep learning.
A lakehouse layering pattern: **Bronze** (raw) → **Silver** (cleaned) → **Gold** (business-ready aggregates). Each layer rebuilds from the prior one.
A single statement that inserts new rows and updates existing ones based on a key. Key to idempotent loads and SCD Type 2.
Massively Parallel Processing — splitting work across many nodes that each handle a slice of data, then combining results. How warehouses query terabytes fast.
A model loosely inspired by brain cells, built from layers of connected 'neurons'. 'Deep' = many layers. The basis of deep learning.
Organising tables so each fact is stored once, removing redundancy (1NF/2NF/3NF). Standard for operational databases. Opposite of denormalization.
Databases that don't use the strict table model — documents (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), wide-column (Cassandra), graph. Built for flexibility/scale.
OLTP = operational systems (many tiny reads/writes, e.g. an app's database). OLAP = analytical systems (few huge reads, e.g. a warehouse).
Cheap, virtually unlimited cloud storage for files of any type (S3, ADLS, GCS). The foundation of a data lake.
Scheduling, sequencing, retrying, and monitoring many pipelines and their dependencies. Main tool: Airflow. See [[DAG]].
A compressed, typed, **columnar** binary file format — the default for analytical data in lakes and Spark. Far faster/cheaper than CSV.
A chunk of a dataset processed independently/in parallel (Spark), or a physical split of a table by a column like date (warehouse) for faster, cheaper queries.
See [[Data pipeline]].
Designing the instructions given to an LLM to get better, more reliable outputs — being specific, giving examples, asking for structure.
The Python interface to Apache Spark, used to process big data across a cluster with a DataFrame API. See [[Spark]].
The dominant programming language for data and AI — readable, beginner-friendly, with libraries for everything (pandas, PySpark, PyTorch).
Retrieval-Augmented Generation — retrieve relevant info (via embeddings + vector search) and feed it to an LLM so it answers from *your* data. See [[Embedding]].
Resilient Distributed Dataset — Spark's low-level distributed collection. Mostly superseded by the optimised DataFrame API.
The structure/blueprint of data: table names, columns, types, and relationships.
Slowly Changing Dimension — strategies for handling changes to dimension data over time. Type 1 = overwrite; Type 2 = add a versioned row (keep history).
Moving data across the network in Spark so matching keys land together (during joins/groupBy). Expensive; minimising it is key to performance.
A popular cloud data **warehouse** that separates storage from compute, so you scale and pay for each independently. (Also a schema type — see star vs snowflake.)
Apache Spark — the standard engine for processing big data in parallel across a cluster. Use via PySpark/Spark SQL. See [[Shuffle]].
Structured Query Language — the readable language for asking questions of and managing relational databases. The #1 must-learn data skill.
A dimensional model with a central fact table joined to surrounding dimension tables. Simple and fast — the default for analytics.
Processing data continuously, event by event, in milliseconds/seconds — for real-time needs like fraud detection. See [[Kafka]].
A meaningless system-generated id (1,2,3…) used as a primary key in warehouses — stable across source changes and essential for SCD Type 2.
The unit an LLM reads/writes — roughly ¾ of a word. Costs and limits are measured in tokens. See [[Context window]].
Transformations (filter, join) are lazy — they build a plan. Actions (count, write) trigger execution. Laziness lets Spark optimise the whole plan.
A database that stores **embeddings** and quickly finds the most similar ones to a query vector. Powers semantic search and RAG (pgvector, FAISS, Pinecone).
In incremental loads: the marker of how far data has been processed (e.g. max updated_at). In streaming: how long to wait for late events before closing a window.
A SQL function computing across related rows *without collapsing* them (running totals, ranking, lag/lead). Pattern: `func() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)`.
